## Review text

DOI: [10.7554/eLife.100337.3.sa1](https://doi.org/10.7554/eLife.100337.3.sa1)

The results of these experiments support a modest but important conclusion: If sub-optimal methods are used to collect retrospective reports, such as simple yes/no questions, inattentional blindness (IB) rates may be overestimated by up to ~8%.

(1) In experiment 1, data from 374 subjects were included in the analysis. As shown in figure 2b, 267 subjects reported noticing the critical stimulus and 107 subjects reported not noticing it. This translates to a 29% IB rate if we were to only consider the "did you notice anything unusual Y/N" question. As reported in the results text (and figure 2c), when asked to report the location of the critical stimulus (left/right), 63.6% of the "non-noticer" group answered correctly. In other words, 68 subjects were correct about the location while 39 subjects were incorrect. Importantly, because the location judgment was a 2-alternative-forced-choice, the assumption was that if 50% (or at least not statistically different than 50%) of the subjects answered the location question correctly, everyone was purely guessing. Therefore, we can estimate that ~39 of the subjects who answered correctly were simply guessing (because 39 guessed incorrectly), leaving 29 subjects from the non-noticer group who were correct on the 2AFC above and beyond the pure guess rate. If these 29 subjects are moved from the non-noticer to the noticer group, the corrected rate of IB for Experiment 1 is 20.86% instead of the original 28.61% rate that would have been obtained if only the Y/N question was used. In other words, relying only on the "Y/N did you notice anything" question led to an overestimate of IB rates by 7.75% in Experiment 1.

In the revised version of their manuscript, the authors provided the data that was missing from the original submission, which allows this same exercise to be carried out on the other 4 experiments. Using the same logic as above, i.e., calculating the pure-guess rate on the 2AFC, moving the number of subjects above this pure-guess rate to the non-noticer group, and then re-calculating a "corrected IB rate", the other experiments demonstrate the following:

Experiment 2: IB rates were overestimated by 4.74% (original IB rate based only on Y/N question = 27.73%; corrected IB rate that includes the 2AFC = 22.99%)

Experiment 3: IB rates were overestimated by 3.58% (original IB rate = 30.85%; corrected IB rate = 27.27%)

Experiment 4: IB rates were overestimated by ~8.19% (original IB rate = 57.32%; corrected IB rate for color* = 39.71%, corrected IB rate for shape = 52.61%, corrected IB rate for location = 55.07%)

Experiment 5: IB rates were overestimated by ~1.44% (original IB rate = 28.99%; corrected IB rate for color = 27.56%, corrected IB rate for shape = 26.43%, corrected IB rate for location = 28.65%)

*note: the highest overestimate of IB rates was from Experiment 4, color condition, but the authors admitted that there was a problem with 2AFC color guessing bias in this version of the experiment which was a main motivation for running experiment 5 which corrected for this bias.

Taken as a whole, this data clearly demonstrates that even with a conservative approach to analyzing the combination of Y/N and 2AFC data, inattentional blindness was evident in a sizeable portion of the subject populations. An important (albeit modest) overestimate of IB rates was demonstrated by incorporating these improved methods.

(2) One of the strongest pieces of evidence presented in this paper was the single data point in Figure 3e showing that in Experiment 3, even the super subject group that rated their non-noticing as "highly confident" had a d' score significantly above zero. Asking for confidence ratings is certainly an improvement over simple Y/N questions about noticing, and if this result were to hold, it could provide a key challenge to IB. However, this result can most likely be explained by measurement error.

In their revised paper, the authors reported data that was missing from their original submission: the confidence ratings on the 2AFC judgments that followed the initial Y/N question. The most striking indication that this data is likely due to measurement error comes from the number of subjects who indicated that they were highly confident that they didn't notice anything on the critical trial, but then when asked to guess the location of the stimulus, indicated that they were highly confident that the stimulus was on the left (or right). There were 18 subjects (8.82% of the high-confidence non-noticer group) who responded this way. To most readers, this combination of responses (high confidence in correctly judging a stimulus feature that one is highly confident in having not seen at all) indicates that a portion of subjects misunderstood the confidence scales (or just didn't read the questions carefully or made mistakes in their responses, which is common for experiments conducted online).

In the authors' rebuttal to the first round of peer review, they wrote, "it is perfectly rationally coherent to be very confident that one didn't see anything but also very confident that if there was anything to be seen, it was on the left." I respectfully disagree that such a combination of responses is rationally coherent. The more parsimonious interpretation is that a measurement error occurred, and it's questionable whether we should trust any responses from these 18 subjects.

In their rebuttal, the authors go on to note that 14 of the 18 subjects who rated their 2AFC with high confidence were correct in their location judgment. If these 14 subjects were removed from analysis (which seems like a reasonable analysis choice, given their contradictory responses), d' for the high-confidence non-noticer group would most likely fall to chance levels. In other words, we would see a data pattern similar to that plotted in Figure 3e, but with the first data point on the left moving down to zero d'. This corrected Figure 3e would then provide a very nice evidence-based justification for including confidence ratings along with Y/N questions in future inattentional blindness studies.

(3) In most (if not all) IB experiments in the literature, a partial attention and/or full attention trial is administered after the critical trial. These control trials are very important for validating IB on the critical trial, as they must show that, when attended, the critical stimuli are very easy to see. If a subject cannot detect the critical stimulus on the control trial, one cannot conclude that they were inattentionally blind on the critical trial, e.g., perhaps the stimulus was just too difficult to see (e.g., too weak, too brief, too far in the periphery, too crowded by distractor stimuli, etc.), or perhaps they weren't paying enough attention overall or failed to follow instructions. In the aggregate data, rates of noticing the stimuli should increase substantially from the critical trial to the control trials. If noticing rates are equivalent on the critical and control trials, one cannot conclude that attention was manipulated in the first place.

In their rebuttal to the first round of peer review, the authors provided weak justification for not including such a control condition. They cite one paper that argues such control conditions are often used to exclude subjects from analysis (those who fail to notice the stimulus on the control trial are either removed from analysis or replaced with new subjects) and such exclusions/replacements can lead to underestimations of inattentional blindness rates. However, the inclusion of a partial or full attention condition as a control does not necessitate the extra step of excluding or replacing subjects. In the broadest sense, such a control condition simply validates the attention manipulation, i.e., one can easily compare the percent of subjects who answered "yes" or who got the 2AFC judgment correct during the critical trial versus the control trial. The subsequent choice about exclusion/replacement is separate, and researchers can always report the data with and without such exclusions/replacements to remain more neutral on this practice.

If anyone were to follow-up on this study, I highly recommend including a partial or full attention control condition, especially given the online nature of data collection. It's important to know the percent of online subjects who answer yes and who get the 2AFC question correct when the critical stimulus is attended, because that is the baseline (in this case, the "ceiling level" of performance) to which the IB rates on the critical trial can be compared.

## Review text

DOI: [10.7554/eLife.100337.3.sa2](https://doi.org/10.7554/eLife.100337.3.sa2)

In this study, Nartker et al. examine how much observers are conscious of using variations of classic inattentional blindness studies. The key idea is that rather than simply ask observers if they noticed a critical object with one yes/no question, the authors also ask follow-up questions to determine if observers are aware of more than the yes/no questions suggest. Specifically, by having observers make forced choice guesses about the critical object, the authors find that many observers who initially said "no" they did not see the object can still "guess" above chance about the critical object's location, color, etc. Thus, the authors claim, that prior claims of inattentional blindness are mistaken and that using such simple methods has led numerous researchers to overestimate how little observers see in the world. To quote the authors themselves, these results imply that "inattentionally blind subjects consciously perceive these stimuli after all... they show sensitivity to IB stimuli because they can see them."

Before getting to a few issues I have with the paper, I do want to make sure to explicitly compliment the researchers for many aspects of their work. Getting massive amounts of data, using signal detection measures, and the novel use of a "super subject" are all important contributions to the literature that I hope are employed more in the future.

Main point 1: My primary issue with this work is that I believe the authors are misrepresenting the way people often perform inattentional blindness studies. In effect, the authors are saying, "People do the studies 'incorrectly' and report that people see very little. We perform the studies 'correctly' and report that people see much more than previously thought." But the way previous studies are conducted is not accurately described in this paper. The authors describe previous studies as follows on page 3:

"Crucially, however, this interpretation of IB and the many implications that follow from it rest on a measure that psychophysics has long recognized to be problematic: simply asking participants whether they noticed anything unusual. In IB studies, awareness of the unexpected stimulus (the novel shape, the parading gorilla, etc.) is retroactively probed with a yes/no question, standardly, "Did you notice anything unusual on the last trial which wasn't there on previous trials?". Any subject who answers "no" is assumed not to have any awareness of the unexpected stimulus.

If this quote were true, the authors would have a point. Unfortunately, I do not believe it is true. This is simply not how many inattentional blindness studies are run. Some of the most famous studies in the inattentional blindness literature do not simply as observes a yes/no question e.g., the invisible gorilla (Simons et al. 1999), the classic door study where the person changes (Simons and Levin, 1998), the study where observers do not notice a fight happening a few feet from them (Chabris et al., 2011). Instead, these papers consistently ask a series of follow-up questions and even tell the observers what just occurred to confirm that observers did not notice that critical event (e.g., "If I were to tell you we just did XYZ, did you notice that?"). In fact, after a brief search on Google Scholar, I was able to relatively quickly find over a dozen papers that do not just use a yes/no procedure, and instead as a series of multiple questions to determine if someone is inattentionally blind. In no particular order some papers:

(1) Most et al. (2005) Psych Review

(2) Drew et al. (2013) Psych Science

(3) Drew et al. (2016) Journal of Vision

(4) Simons et al. (1999) Perception

(5) Simons and Levin (1998) Perception

(6) Chabris et al. (2011) iPerception

(7) Ward & Scholl (2015) Psych Bulletin and Review

(8) Most et al. (2001) Psych Science

(9) Todd & Marois (2005) Psych Science

(10) Fougnie & Marois (2007) Psych Bulletin and Review

(11) New and German (2015) Evolution and Human Behaviour

(12) Jackson-Nielsen (2017) Consciousness and cognition

(13) Mack et al. (2016) Consciousness and cognition

(14) Devue et al. (2009) Perception

(15) Memmert (2014) Cognitive Development

(16) Moore & Egeth (1997) JEP:HPP

(17) Cohen et al. (2020) Proc Natl Acad Sci

(18) Cohen et al. (2011) Psych Science

This is a critical point. The authors' key idea is that when you ask more than just a simple yes/no question, you find that other studies have overestimated the effects of inattentional blindness. But none of the studies listed above only asked simple yes/no questions. Thus, I believe the authors are mis-representing the field. Moreover, many of the studies that do much more than ask a simple yes/no question are cited by the authors themselves! Furthermore, as far as I can tell, the authors believe that if researchers do these extra steps and ask more follow-ups, then the results are valid. But since so many of these prior studies do those extra steps, I am not exactly sure what is being criticized.

To make sure this point is clear, I'd like to use a paper of mine as an example. In this study (Cohen et al., 2020, Proc Natl Acad Sci USA) we used gaze-contingent virtual reality to examine how much color people see in the world. On the critical trial, the part of the scene they fixated on was in color, but the periphery was entirely in black and white. As soon as the trial ended, we asked participants a series of questions to determine what they noticed. The list of questions included:

(1) "Did you notice anything strange or different about that last trial?"

(2) "If I were to tell you that we did something odd on the last trial, would you have a guess as to what we did?"

(3) "If I were to tell you we did something different in the second half of the last trial, would you have a guess as to what we did?"

(4) "Did you notice anything different about the colors in the last scene?"

(5) We then showed observers the previous trial again and drew their attention to the effect and confirmed that they did not notice that previously.

In a situation like this, when the observers are asked so many questions, do the authors believe that "the inattentionally blind can see after all?" I believe they would not say that and the reason they would not say that is because of the follow-up questions after the initial yes/no question. But since so many previous studies use similar follow-up questions, I do not think you can state that the field is broadly overestimating inattentional blindness. This is why it seems to me to be a bit of a straw-man: most people do not just use the yes/no method.

Main point 2: Let's imagine for a second that every study did just ask a yes/no question and then would stop. So, the criticism the authors are bringing up is valid (even though I believe it is not). I am not entirely sure that above chance performance on a forced choice task proves that the inattentionally blind can see after all. Could it just be a form of subliminal priming? Could there be a significant number of participants who basically would say something like, "No I did not see anything, and I feel like I am just guessing, but if you want me to say whether the thing was to the left or right, I will just 100% guess"? I know the literature on priming from things like change and inattentional blindness is a bit unclear, but this seems like maybe what is going on. In fact, maybe the authors are getting some of the best priming from inattentional blindness because of their large sample size, which previous studies do not use.

I'm curious how the authors would relate their studies to masked priming. In masked priming studies, observers say the did not see the target (like in this study) but still are above chance when forced to guess (like in this study). Do the researchers here think that that is evidence of "masked stimuli are truly seen" even if a participant openly says they are guessing?

Main point 3: My last question is about how the authors interpret a variety of inattentional blindness findings. Previous work has found that observers fail to notice a gorilla in a CT scan (Drew et al., 2013), a fight occurring right in front of them (Chabris et al., 2011), a plane on a runway that pilots crash into (Haines, 1991), and so forth. In a situation like this, do the authors believe that many participants are truly aware of these items but simply failed to answer a yes/no question correctly? For example, imagine the researchers made participants choose if the gorilla was in the left or right lung and some participants who initially said they did not notice the gorilla were still able to correctly say if it was in the left or right lung. Would the authors claim "that participant actually did see the gorilla in the lung"? I ask because it is difficult to understand what it means to be aware of something as salient as a gorilla in a CT scan, but say "no" you didn't notice it when asked a yes/no question. What does it mean to be aware of such important, ecologically relevant stimuli, but not act in response to them and openly say "no" you did not notice them?

Overall: I believe there are many aspects of this set of studies that are innovative and I hope the methods will be used more broadly in the literature. However, I believe the authors misrepresent the field and overstate what can be interpreted from their results. While I am sure there are cases where more nuanced questions might reveal inattentional blindness is somewhat overestimated, claims like "the inattentionally blind can see after all" or "Inattentionally blind subjects consciously perceive thest stimuli after all" seem to be incorrect (or at least not at all proven by this data).

results.result: Inattentional blindness (IB) is a well-established, robust phenomenon in perception science where observers fail to report clearly visible stimuli when attention is otherwise engaged, with IB rates reaching over 80% in some studies.
results.evaluation: Claims C1, C9, C10, and C11 collectively establish IB as a foundational phenomenon in the field, supported by extensive citations spanning half a century of research. These claims accurately characterize the existing literature and are well-documented.

results.result: According to the consensus view, IB demonstrates that subjects have no awareness of unattended stimuli, providing key evidence that awareness requires attention and serving as a tool to identify neural correlates of consciousness.
results.evaluation: Claims C12-C14, C2, and C3 accurately represent the orthodox interpretation of IB in the literature, supported by multiple citations to influential theories and neuroscience studies. This characterization of the field's dominant view is well-documented.

results.result: The traditional IB measure (yes/no questions about noticing) is inherently biased because it requires observers to set a criterion, and observers may be conservative in IB tasks due to under-confidence or concern about appearing inattentive, yet this hypothesis remains empirically unsettled.
results.evaluation: Claims C4, C15-C19, and C21 establish the theoretical motivation for the study based on signal detection theory principles. The critique of yes/no questions is well-grounded in psychophysics literature (C15, C16), and the speculative explanations (C18, C19) are appropriately framed as hypotheses to be tested.

results.result: Prior work on residual sensitivity in IB has been criticized for methodological problems including underpowered samples, publication bias, and biased follow-up questions, with a recent meta-analysis calling for well-powered pre-registered experiments.
results.evaluation: Claims C22 and C46-C49 provide a critical assessment of prior literature, supported by citations to a meta-analysis (C22, C49) and specific methodological critiques (C46-C48). The characterization of prior work's limitations is appropriately documented and justified.

results.result: The study employed canonical IB paradigms with 25,000 subjects, introduced a novel 'super subject' signal detection analysis, eschewed divided attention trials, and pre-registered all procedures with public data availability.
results.evaluation: Claims C23, C24, C41, C42, C44, C66, and C67 describe the study's methodological approach. The large sample size (C23), novel analytical approach (C24, C44), adherence to canonical paradigms (C41), and pre-registration (C66, C67) are clearly documented and represent methodological strengths.

results.result: In Experiment 1, 28.6% of subjects were non-noticers, yet 63.6% of non-noticers correctly identified the location of the stimulus they denied noticing (d′₂afc = 0.51, 95% CI = [0.16, 0.85]).
results.evaluation: Claims C25-C27 report Experiment 1 results with appropriate statistical analysis including confidence intervals and Bayes factors. The finding of above-chance performance in non-noticers is clearly demonstrated with proper SDT measures. The data directly support the claim of residual sensitivity.

results.result: In Experiment 2, non-noticers demonstrated above-chance color sensitivity (d′ = 0.38, 95% CI = [0.03, 0.73]) despite a significant response bias favoring 'blue' (c = 0.67), and subjects showed conservative reporting bias on the awareness question (c = 0.31, 95% CI = [0.22, 0.41]).
results.evaluation: Claims C28-C31 report Experiment 2 results including both sensitivity and bias measures. The introduction of absent trials (C31) provides the first direct evidence of conservative reporting bias in IB. The statistical analyses are appropriate and confidence intervals support the conclusions.

results.result: In Experiment 3, even high-confidence non-noticers (those rating confidence as '3' that they didn't notice anything) collectively showed above-chance location sensitivity (d′₂afc = 0.34, 95% CI = [0.08, 0.60]), and confidence predicted discrimination accuracy.
results.evaluation: Claims C32 and C33 demonstrate that residual sensitivity persists even in the most confident non-noticers (N=204), strengthening the main finding. The confidence-accuracy relationship (C33) is supported by Figure 3e and suggests graded awareness, though this is appropriately framed as suggestive rather than definitive.

results.result: In Experiment 4 using a sustained IB paradigm, 57.3% showed IB, yet non-noticers demonstrated above-chance sensitivity to color (d′ = 0.82) and shape (d′ = 0.21), with conservative reporting bias (c = 0.85), though color-incongruent stimuli showed higher IB rates (86.57% vs 28.71%).
results.evaluation: Claims C34-C37 extend findings to dynamic stimuli with 5-second presentations. The color congruency effect (C37) is appropriately identified as a potential confound that may inflate color sensitivity estimates, demonstrating critical self-assessment. The conservative bias is even stronger than in Experiment 2.

results.result: Experiment 5, the largest single IB study ever (10,830 subjects, 2,339 non-noticers), controlled for color congruency using orange/green stimuli and found non-noticers performed above-chance on color (d′ = 0.12) and shape (d′ = 0.23) but not location, with conservative reporting bias (c = 0.45).
results.evaluation: Claims C38-C40, C87-C89 describe Experiment 5, which addresses the color congruency confound from Experiment 4. The massive sample size (C40) provides strong statistical power. The pattern replicates Experiment 4 with reduced but still significant color sensitivity, supporting the robustness of the main findings.

results.result: The 'super subject' SDT analysis makes assumptions about criterion stability and equal variance that could affect estimates, but violations would be slight and the log-linear correction (adding 0.5 to all cells) provides conservative estimates of d′.
results.evaluation: Claims C45, C90, and C92 address methodological assumptions transparently. The authors provide calculations showing that violations of equal variance would have minimal impact on conclusions (C45), and note that the log-linear correction underestimates d′ if anything (C90), demonstrating appropriate methodological rigor.

results.result: Across five experiments, inattentionally blind participants collectively demonstrated above-chance sensitivity to location, color, and shape of stimuli they denied noticing, with systematic conservative reporting bias, providing the strongest evidence to date of residual visual sensitivity in IB.
results.evaluation: Claims C5-C7 and C61 summarize the main findings across all experiments. The convergent evidence from five pre-registered experiments with over 25,000 subjects, using both brief and sustained presentations, provides strong support for residual sensitivity and conservative bias in IB.

results.result: The findings challenge the orthodox interpretation that IB reflects complete absence of awareness and the use of IB to argue that awareness requires attention, suggesting instead that awareness of certain features may survive inattention.
results.evaluation: Claims C8, C20, C62, and C63 draw theoretical implications from the empirical findings. The challenge to the orthodox view is logically supported by the demonstration of residual sensitivity and conservative bias. However, the strength of this challenge depends on whether above-chance performance reflects conscious or unconscious processing (addressed in C55-C56).

results.result: The results offer an alternative explanation for prior findings of neural and behavioral processing in IB (that subjects retain awareness rather than unconscious processing), though above-chance performance could reflect unconscious representations; the authors argue explicit judgments constitute prima facie evidence of conscious processing.
results.evaluation: Claims C54-C58 address the critical question of whether residual sensitivity reflects conscious or unconscious processing. While the authors provide a theoretical argument (C56) and acknowledge alternatives (C55), this remains a matter of interpretation rather than direct empirical demonstration. The compatibility with inattentional amnesia (C57-C58) is appropriately nuanced.

results.result: The findings support a graded perspective on perception and awareness, suggesting that inattention degrades rather than eliminates perception and awareness, challenging binary conceptualizations.
results.evaluation: Claims C59, C60, and C65 propose a theoretical reframing based on the empirical findings. The graded perspective is supported by the pattern of partial sensitivity across features and the confidence-accuracy relationship (C33), though this represents an inference from the data rather than direct measurement of graded awareness.

results.result: The study provides the well-powered pre-registered evidence called for by recent meta-analyses and highlights the value of assessing response bias and objective sensitivity measures in studying IB and visual awareness.
results.evaluation: Claims C50 and C64 position the study's contribution relative to prior work and methodological recommendations. The study clearly addresses the limitations identified in the meta-analysis (C22, C49) through pre-registration, large samples, and SDT analysis, representing a significant methodological advance.

results.result: Prior research has found preserved neural signatures (Nd1 ERP, scene segmentation) and behavioral effects in inattentionally blind subjects, which have been interpreted as subliminal processing.
results.evaluation: Claims C51-C53 accurately summarize prior neuroscience and behavioral findings with appropriate citations. These claims provide context for the current study's alternative interpretation (C54) but do not constitute new findings from this work.

results.result: Non-noticers demonstrated above-chance sensitivity to stimulus features (location, color, shape) in forced-choice discrimination tasks across all five experiments, with d' values ranging from 0.12 to 0.82 depending on the feature and experiment.
results.evaluation: Reviewer 1 acknowledges the above-chance performance but argues this represents only a 'modest' overestimate of IB rates (1.44-8.19%) when corrected, suggesting 'inattentional blindness was evident in a sizeable portion of the subject populations.' Reviewer 3 questions whether above-chance performance proves conscious perception, suggesting it could reflect 'subliminal priming' rather than awareness, analogous to masked priming studies. The editor notes the findings are 'convincing' but reviewers fundamentally disagree on interpretation.

results.result: Subjects were collectively biased to respond 'no' to the yes/no awareness question, with conservative criterion values (c) ranging from 0.31 to 0.85 across experiments with absent trials.
results.evaluation: The editor explicitly states 'the authors show that this is because participants are generally conservative and biased to report not noticing in inattentional blindness experiments.' Reviewer 1 accepts this finding as demonstrating 'an important (albeit modest) overestimate of IB rates.' No reviewer challenges the bias finding itself, though they dispute its theoretical implications.

results.result: High-confidence non-noticers in Experiment 3 demonstrated above-chance sensitivity to location (d' = 0.34), and confidence ratings predicted discrimination accuracy, suggesting graded awareness.
results.evaluation: Reviewer 1 argues this result 'can most likely be explained by measurement error,' noting that 18 subjects (8.82%) were highly confident they didn't notice anything but also highly confident in their location judgment—a 'contradictory' pattern suggesting subjects 'misunderstood the confidence scales.' Reviewer 1 states that removing these 14 correct subjects would likely reduce d' to chance levels, making this 'the strongest piece of evidence' actually unreliable.

results.result: The authors claim that prior IB studies rely on biased yes/no questions that are 'notoriously subject to bias' and that follow-up questions in prior studies remain subject to the same bias problems.
results.evaluation: Reviewer 3 strongly challenges this characterization, stating 'I believe the authors are misrepresenting the way people often perform inattentional blindness studies.' Reviewer 3 provides 18 examples of studies that 'do not just use a yes/no procedure, and instead ask a series of multiple questions,' including many cited by the authors themselves. Reviewer 3 concludes this is 'a bit of a straw-man: most people do not just use the yes/no method.'

results.result: The study eschewed divided and full attention control trials, citing controversy about whether such exclusions understate IB prevalence.
results.evaluation: Reviewer 1 states the authors 'provided weak justification for not including such a control condition,' arguing that control trials are 'very important for validating IB on the critical trial' to ensure stimuli are detectable when attended. Reviewer 1 notes that 'the inclusion of a partial or full attention condition as a control does not necessitate the extra step of excluding or replacing subjects' and 'highly recommend[s] including' such controls, especially for online data collection.

results.result: The findings challenge the orthodox interpretation that IB reflects complete absence of awareness and that awareness requires attention, suggesting instead that inattentionally blind subjects retain some degree of awareness.
results.evaluation: Reviewer 1 characterizes the conclusion as 'modest but important' (IB rates overestimated by ~8%), not a fundamental challenge to IB. Reviewer 3 states claims like 'the inattentionally blind can see after all' are 'incorrect (or at least not at all proven by this data)' and questions what it means to be 'aware' of salient stimuli like a gorilla while saying 'no' you didn't notice it. Reviewer 3 suggests the data could reflect subliminal processing rather than conscious awareness.

results.result: The study employed novel methodology including massive sample sizes (25,000 subjects total), pre-registration, signal detection theory analysis, and a 'super subject' approach to overcome single-trial limitations.
results.evaluation: The editor notes 'the samples sizes are large and the analysis protocol is novel.' Reviewer 3 explicitly compliments 'getting massive amounts of data, using signal detection measures, and the novel use of a "super subject"' as 'important contributions to the literature that I hope are employed more in the future.' All reviewers acknowledge the methodological innovations even while disputing interpretations.

results.result: In Experiment 4, the IB rate for color-incongruent stimuli was substantially higher than for color-congruent stimuli (86.57% vs 28.71%), suggesting attentional suppression occurred.
results.evaluation: Reviewer 1 acknowledges 'there was a problem with 2AFC color guessing bias in this version of the experiment which was a main motivation for running experiment 5 which corrected for this bias.' This implicit acceptance of the color congruency effect and the authors' correction in Experiment 5 indicates the finding is recognized as valid, though it raised methodological concerns addressed in subsequent experiments.

results.result: The authors argue that explicit voluntary judgments of stimulus features constitute prima facie evidence of conscious processing rather than unconscious representations akin to blindsight.
results.evaluation: Reviewer 3 directly challenges this interpretation, asking whether above-chance performance could be 'a form of subliminal priming' and drawing parallels to masked priming where 'observers say they did not see the target (like in this study) but still are above chance when forced to guess.' Reviewer 3 questions whether the authors would claim 'masked stimuli are truly seen' in such cases, highlighting fundamental disagreement about what the forced-choice performance indicates about consciousness.

comparisons.comparison: Both evaluate claims C32-C33 about residual sensitivity in highly confident non-noticers. OpenEval finds this SUPPORTED as strengthening the main finding, while peer reviewers find it UNSUPPORTED, arguing the result likely reflects measurement error from subjects who misunderstood confidence scales. This represents fundamental disagreement on data quality.

Both address claims C8, C20, C62-C63 about theoretical implications challenging the orthodox view of IB. OpenEval finds these SUPPORTED (with caveats about interpretation), while peer reviewers find them UNSUPPORTED, characterizing the challenge as modest (~8% overestimate) rather than fundamental, and questioning whether above-chance performance proves conscious awareness versus subliminal processing.

Both evaluate claims C55-C56 about whether residual sensitivity reflects conscious versus unconscious processing. OpenEval rates this UNCERTAIN, acknowledging it remains interpretive rather than empirically demonstrated. Peer reviewers also rate it UNCERTAIN, suggesting above-chance performance could reflect subliminal priming analogous to masked priming studies, highlighting fundamental ambiguity about what forced-choice performance indicates.

Both address claims C4, C15-C17 about the theoretical motivation and critique of yes/no questions in prior IB research. OpenEval finds this SUPPORTED as well-grounded in psychophysics literature. Peer reviewers find it UNSUPPORTED, arguing the authors misrepresent the field by creating a straw-man, citing 18 studies (including some the authors cite) that use multiple questions rather than simple yes/no procedures.

OpenEval R4 addresses claims C22, C46-C49 about methodological critiques of prior literature, finding them SUPPORTED. Peer R4 overlaps on C46-C48 but finds the characterization UNSUPPORTED, arguing it's a straw-man since most studies don't just use yes/no methods. This represents disagreement on how accurately the authors characterize existing literature.

Both evaluate methodological claims including large sample sizes (C23), novel analytical approach (C24, C44), and pre-registration (C66). Both find these SUPPORTED. OpenEval emphasizes these as methodological strengths, while peer reviewers explicitly compliment the massive data collection, signal detection measures, and 'super subject' approach as important contributions to the field.

OpenEval R5 includes claim C42 about adherence to canonical paradigms as SUPPORTED. Peer R5 addresses C42-C43 about lack of control conditions, finding this UNSUPPORTED with weak justification, arguing control trials are important for validating IB and ensuring stimuli detectability when attended. This represents disagreement on experimental design adequacy.

Both address Experiment 1 results (C25-C27 in OpenEval, C26-C27 in peer review). OpenEval finds the above-chance performance SUPPORTED with proper statistical analysis. Peer reviewers rate it UNCERTAIN, acknowledging above-chance performance but characterizing it as only a 'modest' overestimate (1.44-8.19%) and questioning whether it proves conscious perception versus subliminal priming.

Both evaluate conservative reporting bias findings. OpenEval R7 addresses C28-C31 including bias evidence (C31), finding it SUPPORTED. Peer R2 addresses C6, C31, C36, C39 about bias, also finding it SUPPORTED. Both agree the bias finding itself is convincing, though peer reviewers dispute its theoretical implications for the nature of IB.

Both address claim C37 about the color congruency effect in Experiment 4. OpenEval finds it SUPPORTED, noting the authors appropriately identified this potential confound. Peer reviewers also implicitly accept it as SUPPORTED, acknowledging the problem and the authors' correction in Experiment 5, though it raised methodological concerns.

OpenEval R12 addresses main findings summary (C5-C7, C61) as SUPPORTED by convergent evidence. Peer R1 includes C5 in their UNCERTAIN evaluation, acknowledging above-chance performance but characterizing the overall effect as modest. Both address the core empirical findings but differ on magnitude and interpretation.

OpenEval R12 includes C6 (conservative bias) in summary of main findings as SUPPORTED. Peer R2 also addresses C6 as SUPPORTED, with the editor explicitly stating authors show participants are conservative and biased. Both agree on this finding, representing a key area of concordance.

OpenEval finds claims C1, C9-C11 about IB as a foundational phenomenon SUPPORTED by extensive citations. No corresponding peer review evaluation found for these background/literature characterization claims.

OpenEval finds claims C12-C14, C2-C3 about the orthodox interpretation of IB SUPPORTED as accurately representing the field's dominant view. No corresponding peer review evaluation found for this characterization of existing theory.

OpenEval finds claims C38-C40, C87-C89 about Experiment 5 (addressing color congruency confound) SUPPORTED with massive sample size and replication of patterns. No direct peer review evaluation found, though peer R8 acknowledges the motivation for this experiment.

OpenEval finds claims C45, C90, C92 about methodological assumptions (equal variance, log-linear correction) SUPPORTED, noting transparent treatment. No corresponding peer review evaluation found for these technical methodological details.

OpenEval finds claims C59-C60, C65 about theoretical reframing toward graded perspective SUPPORTED by pattern of partial sensitivity and confidence-accuracy relationship. No corresponding peer review evaluation found for this specific theoretical proposal.

OpenEval finds claims C50, C64 about methodological contributions and recommendations SUPPORTED, noting the study addresses limitations from prior meta-analysis. No corresponding peer review evaluation found, though peer R7 compliments methodological innovations.

OpenEval finds claims C51-C53 summarizing prior neuroscience and behavioral findings SUPPORTED as accurate literature summary. No corresponding peer review evaluation found for these contextual background claims.
